claim: Fibroblast Growth Factors (FGF) 9 and 20 are expressed in the non-sensory (Fgf9) and sensory (Fgf20) epithelium during otic development.
source: Here, we show that Fibroblast Growth Factors (FGF) 9 and 20, which are expressed in the non-sensory (Fgf9) and sensory (Fgf20) epithelium during otic development, regulate the number of cochlear progenitors.
evidence: Supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 1 and referenced prior studies

claim: FGF9 and FGF20 regulate the number of cochlear progenitors.
source: Here, we show that Fibroblast Growth Factors (FGF) 9 and 20, which are expressed in the non-sensory (Fgf9) and sensory (Fgf20) epithelium during otic development, regulate the number of cochlear progenitors.
evidence: Demonstrated through genetic knockout experiments showing decreased progenitor proliferation in Fgf9/Fgf20 double mutants

claim: Fgf receptor (Fgfr) 1 signaling within the developing sensory epithelium is required for the differentiation of outer hair cells and supporting cells.
source: We further demonstrate that Fgf receptor (Fgfr) 1 signaling within the developing sensory epithelium is required for the differentiation of outer hair cells and SCs, while mesenchymal FGFRs regulate the size of the sensory progenitor population and the overall cochlear length.
evidence: Demonstrated through conditional knockout of Fgfr1 in epithelium showing loss of outer hair cells and supporting cells

claim: Mesenchymal FGFRs regulate the size of the sensory progenitor population and the overall cochlear length.
source: We further demonstrate that Fgf receptor (Fgfr) 1 signaling within the developing sensory epithelium is required for the differentiation of outer hair cells and SCs, while mesenchymal FGFRs regulate the size of the sensory progenitor population and the overall cochlear length.
evidence: Demonstrated through conditional knockout of Fgfr1/Fgfr2 in mesenchyme showing decreased cochlear length and progenitor proliferation

claim: Ectopic FGFR activation in mesenchyme is sufficient to increase sensory progenitor proliferation and cochlear length.
source: In addition, ectopic FGFR activation in mesenchyme was sufficient to increase sensory progenitor proliferation and cochlear length.
evidence: Demonstrated through constitutive activation of FGFR1 in mesenchyme showing increased proliferation and cochlear length

claim: The cochlea begins to grow from the ventral otic vesicle at embryonic day 11.5 (E11.5).
source: In mouse, the cochlea begins to grow from the ventral otic vesicle at embryonic day 11.5 (E11.5) and continues to grow and coil, forming approximately one and a half turns by birth.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mouse cochlear development

claim: The cochlea continues to grow and coil, forming approximately one and a half turns by birth.
source: In mouse, the cochlea begins to grow from the ventral otic vesicle at embryonic day 11.5 (E11.5) and continues to grow and coil, forming approximately one and a half turns by birth.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mouse cochlear development

claim: Sensory progenitors exit the cell cycle by E14.5.
source: In mouse, sensory progenitors exit the cell cycle by E14.5 and begin to differentiate into HCs and SCs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cochlear development timeline

claim: The size of the progenitor population at E14.5 is the ultimate determinant of the size of the adult cochlea.
source: Thus, the size of the progenitor population at this stage of development is the ultimate determinant of the size of the adult cochlea.
evidence: Logical inference from the fact that progenitors exit the cell cycle by E14.5 and do not re-enter

claim: Progenitor number is determined by proliferation, the timing of differentiation, and in some cases by aberrant cell death.
source: Progenitor number is determined by proliferation, the timing of differentiation, and in some cases by aberrant cell death.
evidence: Based on general principles of developmental biology

claim: Sensory progenitor growth requires mesenchymal signals.
source: Previous studies indicate that sensory progenitor growth requires mesenchymal signals (Phippard et al., 1999; Montcouquiol and Kelley, 2003; Braunstein et al., 2008, 2009), however, the identity and source of the factors that control this activity are not known.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: FGF3 and FGF10 signal from hindbrain and head mesenchyme, respectively, to the overlying ectoderm to induce formation of the otic placode and vesicle.
source: FGF3 and FGF10 signal from hindbrain and head mesenchyme, respectively, to the overlying ectoderm to induce formation of the otic placode and vesicle (Urness et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: FGF20 regulates differentiation of outer hair cells (OHC) and supporting cells, termed the lateral compartment of the cochlea.
source: Later in development, FGF20 regulates differentiation of outer hair cells (OHC) and SCs, termed the lateral compartment of the cochlea (Huh et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by the authors

claim: FGF20 signals directly to FGFR1, serving as a permissive factor for differentiation.
source: Phenotypic similarities with mice lacking Fgfr1 in the entire otic epithelium suggest that FGF20 signals directly to FGFR1, serving as a permissive factor for differentiation (Pirvola et al., 2002; Hayashi et al., 2008; Huh et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from phenotypic similarities between Fgf20 and Fgfr1 mutants, supported by citations

claim: FGF9 signaling regulates structural components of the vestibular system, but alone has no effect on cochlear development.
source: FGF9 signaling regulates structural components of the vestibular system, but alone has no effect on cochlear development (Pirvola et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: FGF8 signaling from the inner hair cell (IHC) to FGFR3 in supporting cells regulates pillar cell differentiation.
source: During postmitotic stages, FGF8 signaling from the inner hair cell (IHC) to FGFR3 in SCs regulates pillar cell differentiation (Colvin et al., 1996; Mueller et al., 2002; Jacques et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Fgf20 is expressed in a portion of the otic vesicle sensory epithelium beginning at E10.5.
source: However, Fgf20 is expressed in a portion of the otic vesicle sensory epithelium much earlier in development, beginning at E10.5 (Huh et al., 2012), but analysis of mice lacking Fgf20 did not reveal any function for Fgf20 at this stage of development.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by the authors

claim: Fgf9 is expressed in the otic epithelium at E10.5–12.5.
source: Fgf9 is closely related to Fgf20 (Zhang et al., 2006; Itoh and Ornitz, 2008), and is also expressed in the otic epithelium at E10.5–12.5 (Pirvola et al., 2004); however, Fgf9−/− mice have normal cochlear development and normal patterning of the organ of Corti (Pirvola et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Fgf9−/− mice have normal cochlear development and normal patterning of the organ of Corti.
source: Fgf9 is closely related to Fgf20 (Zhang et al., 2006; Itoh and Ornitz, 2008), and is also expressed in the otic epithelium at E10.5–12.5 (Pirvola et al., 2004); however, Fgf9−/− mice have normal cochlear development and normal patterning of the organ of Corti (Pirvola et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: At E10.5, βGal activity was detected in the otic vesicle epithelium in Fgf9lacZ embryos.
source: At E10.5, βGal activity was detected in the otic vesicle epithelium (Figure 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by βGal staining shown in Figure 1A

claim: Fgf9 is expressed in the non-sensory epithelium of the otic vesicle at E11.5.
source: Co-staining of βGal and Sox2 at E11.5 showed no overlap, indicating that Fgf9 is expressed in the non-sensory epithelium of the otic vesicle (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining shown in Figure 1B

claim: Fgf9 and Fgf20 are both expressed in the otic vesicle, but in non-overlapping domains in the otic epithelium.
source: Taken together with previous Fgf20 expression analysis at this stage (Huh et al., 2012, Figure 1C), Fgf9 and Fgf20 are both expressed in the otic vesicle, but in non-overlapping domains in the otic epithelium (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by expression analysis shown in Figures 1B-D and cited previous study

claim: Control embryos (Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/+) showed a normal pattern of three rows of OHCs and one row of IHCs throughout the cochlear duct.
source: Control embryos (Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/+) showed a normal pattern of three rows of OHCs and one row of IHCs throughout the cochlear duct (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by phalloidin and p75 staining shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae showed the same wild type HC pattern as the double heterozygous controls.
source: Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae showed the same wild type HC pattern as the double heterozygous controls (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by phalloidin and p75 staining shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae showed patches of sensory HCs and gaps.
source: Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae showed patches of sensory HCs and gaps (Figure 2A–C) (Huh et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by phalloidin and p75 staining shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae showed a similar patterning phenotype to Fgf20lacZ/lacZ mice.
source: Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae also showed a similar patterning phenotype to Fgf20lacZ/lacZ mice (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by phalloidin, p75, Prox1, and Sox2 staining shown in Figure 2A-D

claim: The density of OHCs in Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae was similar to double heterozygous controls.
source: The density (number of cells per 100 μm) of OHCs in Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae was similar to double heterozygous controls (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 2E

claim: The densities of OHCs in Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae were significantly decreased compared to double heterozygous controls.
source: However, the densities of OHCs in Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae were similar to each other (ANOVA, p > 0.1), and significantly (ANOVA, p < 0.0001) decreased compared to double heterozygous controls (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: Densities of IHCs were comparable in all genotypes.
source: Densities of IHCs were comparable in all genotypes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 2E

claim: In double heterozygous control cochleae, 5 rows of Prox1+ SCs overlapped with Sox2 staining.
source: In double heterozygous control cochleae, 5 rows of Prox1+ SCs overlapped with Sox2 staining (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2D

claim: Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae showed a similar SC pattern to controls.
source: Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae showed a similar pattern (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2D

claim: Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae showed patches of SCs separated by gaps of Sox2+, Prox1− cells.
source: In contrast, Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae showed patches of SCs separated by gaps of Sox2+, Prox1− cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2D

claim: The density of SCs in Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ was comparable to double heterozygous control.
source: The density of SCs in Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ was comparable (ANOVA, p > 0.5) to double heterozygous control (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: The density of SCs in Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ were significantly decreased compared to double heterozygous controls.
source: The density of SCs in Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ were similar to each other (ANOVA, p > 0.3) and significantly (ANOVA, p < 0.0001) decreased compared to double heterozygous controls (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: The length of Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae was comparable to that of double heterozygous controls.
source: The length of Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae was comparable (ANOVA, p > 0.1) to that of double heterozygous controls (Figure 2G), whereas the length of Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was 16% and 18% shorter than double heterozygous controls (p < 0.05 and p < 0.001), respectively, and the length of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was reduced by 58% compared to controls (p < 0.001) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: The length of Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was 16% shorter than double heterozygous controls.
source: The length of Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae was comparable (ANOVA, p > 0.1) to that of double heterozygous controls (Figure 2G), whereas the length of Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was 16% and 18% shorter than double heterozygous controls (p < 0.05 and p < 0.001), respectively, and the length of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was reduced by 58% compared to controls (p < 0.001) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: The length of Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was 18% shorter than double heterozygous controls.
source: The length of Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae was comparable (ANOVA, p > 0.1) to that of double heterozygous controls (Figure 2G), whereas the length of Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was 16% and 18% shorter than double heterozygous controls (p < 0.05 and p < 0.001), respectively, and the length of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was reduced by 58% compared to controls (p < 0.001) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: The length of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was reduced by 58% compared to controls.
source: The length of Fgf9−/− and Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/+ cochleae was comparable (ANOVA, p > 0.1) to that of double heterozygous controls (Figure 2G), whereas the length of Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was 16% and 18% shorter than double heterozygous controls (p < 0.05 and p < 0.001), respectively, and the length of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae was reduced by 58% compared to controls (p < 0.001) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ double knockout cochleae were 49% and 51% of the length of Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae.
source: In addition, Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ double knockout cochleae were 49% and 51% of the length of Fgf20lacZ/lacZ and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae (p < 0.001), respectively (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: Fgf9 and Fgf20 have a redundant role in attaining proper cochlear length.
source: These data identify a redundant role for Fgf9 and Fgf20 to attain the proper cochlear length, while Fgf20, alone, primarily regulates cochlear patterning and differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of both Fgf9 and Fgf20 results in much greater cochlear length reduction than loss of either alone

claim: Fgf20, alone, primarily regulates cochlear patterning and differentiation.
source: These data identify a redundant role for Fgf9 and Fgf20 to attain the proper cochlear length, while Fgf20, alone, primarily regulates cochlear patterning and differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of Fgf20 alone results in patterning defects while loss of Fgf9 alone does not

claim: Cochlear sensory progenitors exit the cell cycle beginning at E12.5 in the apex and progressing towards the base by E14.5.
source: In mouse, cochlear sensory progenitors exit the cell cycle beginning at E12.5 in the apex and progressing towards the base by E14.5 (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The Sox2+ prosensory domain of double heterozygous control and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ inner ears were similar at E14.5.
source: The Sox2+ prosensory domain of double heterozygous control and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ inner ears were similar (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by Sox2 immunostaining shown in Figure 3A

claim: The Sox2+ prosensory domain of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ inner ears were clearly smaller than that of double heterozygous control or Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae at E14.5.
source: However, the Sox2+ prosensory domain of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ inner ears were clearly smaller than that of double heterozygous control or Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by Sox2 immunostaining shown in Figure 3A

claim: The Sox2+ prosensory domain was less compact in Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ inner ears compared to double heterozygous control and inner ears with one wild type allele of Fgf9 at E14.5.
source: Immunostaining of histological sections of E14.5 inner ears showed that the Sox2+ prosensory domain was less compact in Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ inner ears compared to double heterozygous control and inner ears with one wild type allele of Fgf9 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Sox2 immunostaining on sections shown in Figure 3B

claim: p27kip1 showed a very similar pattern to that of Sox2, with more diffuse cells in the prosensory domain of E14.5 inner ears of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ mice.
source: Immunostaining for p27kip1 (Cdkn1b) showed a very similar pattern to that of Sox2, with more diffuse cells in the prosensory domain of E14.5 inner ears of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by p27 immunostaining shown in Figure 3C

claim: Jag1 showed a similar expression pattern across all three genotypes at E14.5, indicating that the medial compartment of the cochlea was correctly specified.
source: Jag1, which marks the medial prosensory cells that will give rise to IHCs, inner SCs, and Kölliker's organ (Ohyama et al., 2010; Basch et al., 2011), showed a similar expression pattern across all three genotypes, indicating that the medial compartment of the cochlea was correctly specified (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Jag1 immunostaining shown in Figure 3D, with inference about medial compartment specification

claim: Proliferation of Sox2+ sensory progenitors was similar in double heterozygous control and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae at E11.5.
source: Quantification of the number of pHH3+, Sox2+ sensory progenitors showed similar numbers (p > 0.09 at E11.5 and p > 0.2 at E12.5) in double heterozygous control and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of pHH3 and Sox2 co-staining shown in Figure 3G

claim: Proliferation of Sox2+ sensory progenitors was similar in double heterozygous control and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae at E12.5.
source: Quantification of the number of pHH3+, Sox2+ sensory progenitors showed similar numbers (p > 0.09 at E11.5 and p > 0.2 at E12.5) in double heterozygous control and Fgf9−/+;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochleae (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of pHH3 and Sox2 co-staining shown in Figure 3H

claim: Proliferation of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochlear epithelial cells was significantly decreased at E11.5 compared to double heterozygous controls.
source: However, proliferation of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochlear epithelial cells was significantly decreased at E11.5 (p < 0.001) and E12.5 (p < 0.01) compared to double heterozygous controls (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of pHH3 and Sox2 co-staining shown in Figure 3G

claim: Proliferation of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochlear epithelial cells was significantly decreased at E12.5 compared to double heterozygous controls.
source: However, proliferation of Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ cochlear epithelial cells was significantly decreased at E11.5 (p < 0.001) and E12.5 (p < 0.01) compared to double heterozygous controls (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of pHH3 and Sox2 co-staining shown in Figure 3H

claim: No cell death (aCasp3+) was detected in any of the genotypes at E11.5 and E12.5.
source: No cell death (aCasp3+) was detected in any of the genotypes at E11.5 and E12.5 (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as experimental observation

claim: Expression of p27kip1 begins at E12.5 in the apex of the cochlea and progresses towards the base.
source: p27kip1 is one of the cell cycle inhibitors that is expressed in sensory progenitors as they become postmitotic. Expression of p27kip1 begins at E12.5 in the apex of the cochlea and progresses towards the base (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: By E14.5, the entire cochlear progenitor domain becomes p27kip1 positive.
source: By E14.5, the entire cochlear progenitor domain becomes p27kip1 positive.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cochlear development

claim: Expression of p27kip1 at E12.5 in the proximal cochlear duct was not detected in either control or Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ embryos.
source: Expression of p27kip1 at E12.5 in the proximal cochlear duct was not detected in either control or Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ embryos suggesting that there is no premature cell cycle exit in mice lacking Fgf9 and Fgf20 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by p27 immunostaining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, with inference about cell cycle exit

claim: Expression of both Fgfr1 and Fgfr2 have been reported in the otic epithelium and periotic mesenchyme between E10.5 and E12.5.
source: Expression of both Fgfr1 and Fgfr2 have been reported in the otic epithelium and periotic mesenchyme between E10.5 and E12.5 (Pirvola et al., 2000, 2002, 2004; Ono et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Epithelial Fgfr1 has been conditionally inactivated in otic epithelium using Foxg1Cre, Six1enh21Cre, and Emx2Cre.
source: Epithelial Fgfr1 has been conditionally inactivated in otic epithelium using Foxg1Cre, Six1enh21Cre, and Emx2Cre (Pirvola et al., 2002; Ono et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Conditional inactivation of Fgfr1 in otic epithelium results in a cochlear epithelium with reduced numbers of HCs, with OHC numbers being more severely affected than IHC numbers.
source: This results in a cochlear epithelium with reduced numbers of HCs, with OHC numbers being more severely affected than IHC numbers.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: A 40–50% decrease in cochlear length was reported when Fgfr1 was inactivated with Six1enh21Cre, or Emx2Cre.
source: In addition to the loss of differentiated HCs, a 40–50% decrease in cochlear length was reported when Fgfr1 was inactivated with Six1enh21Cre, or Emx2Cre (Ono et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The density of OHCs in Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ embryos demonstrated a significant decrease compared to controls.
source: Quantification of the density of OHCs in Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ embryos demonstrated a significant (p < 0.0001) decrease compared to controls (Fgfr1+/f::Foxg1Cre/+) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,E), while the density of IHCs was not changed (p > 0.09).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: The density of IHCs in Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ embryos was not changed compared to controls.
source: Quantification of the density of OHCs in Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ embryos demonstrated a significant (p < 0.0001) decrease compared to controls (Fgfr1+/f::Foxg1Cre/+) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,E), while the density of IHCs was not changed (p > 0.09).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: The length of Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ cochleae was only 9% shorter than control.
source: Furthermore, the length of Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ cochleae was only 9% shorter than control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,F), similar to what was observed in Fgf20lacZ/lacZ embryos (Figures 1B, 2G and ref. Huh et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F

claim: Whole mount Sox2 staining of E14.5 Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ cochleae was comparable to control, indicating that the number of Sox2+ progenitors was not changed.
source: Whole mount Sox2 staining of E14.5 Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ cochleae was also comparable to control, indicating that the number of Sox2+ progenitors was not changed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Sox2 staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, with inference about progenitor number

claim: Proliferation of the Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ prosensory epithelium was comparable to that of controls at E12.5.
source: In addition, proliferation of the Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ prosensory epithelium was comparable (p > 0.6) to that of controls at E12.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of proliferation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G

claim: Fgfr2 is required for formation of the otic vesicle.
source: However, Fgfr2 is required for formation of the otic vesicle and Foxg1Cre, which is active before and during the otic vesicle stage (Hébert and McConnell, 2000), could not be used to investigate the role of Fgfr2 at later stages of otic vesicle development.
evidence: Supported by citation and logical inference about experimental limitations

claim: Cre activity in Fgf20Cre/+;ROSAmTmG/+ mice was detected at E10.5 in a subset of the Sox2+ prosensory domain, in a pattern identical to that of Fgf20lacZ embryos.
source: Cre activity was detected at E10.5 in a subset of the Sox2+ prosensory domain, in a pattern identical to that of Fgf20lacZ embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by lineage tracing shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: At P0, all of the components of the organ of Corti were positive for the Fgf20Cre/+;ROSAmTmG/+ lineage tracer.
source: At P0, all of the components of the organ of Corti were positive for the Fgf20Cre/+;ROSAmTmG/+ lineage tracer, indicating that Fgf20Cre is active in prosensory progenitors or their lineage (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by lineage tracing shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, with inference about Cre activity

claim: The phenotype of Fgfr1−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ cochleae was similar to that of Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, and Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ cochleae.
source: The phenotype of Fgfr1−/f::Fgf20Cre/+(Fgfr1−/f;Fgfr2+/f::Fgf20Cre/+) cochleae was similar to that of Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, Fgf9−/−;Fgf20lacZ/lacZ, and Fgfr1−/f::Foxg1Cre/+ cochleae (Figures 2A–C, 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of staining patterns shown in multiple figures

claim: The pattern and morphology of Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ cochleae was similar to control.
source: In contrast, the pattern and morphology of Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+(Fgfr1+/f;Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+) cochleae was similar to control (Figure 4A–C) and Fgfr1−/f;Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ cochleae was comparable to Fgfr1−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by staining patterns shown in Figure 4A-C

claim: Fgfr1−/f;Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ cochleae was comparable to Fgfr1−/f::Fgf20Cre/+.
source: In contrast, the pattern and morphology of Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+(Fgfr1+/f;Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+) cochleae was similar to control (Figure 4A–C) and Fgfr1−/f;Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ cochleae was comparable to Fgfr1−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by staining patterns shown in Figure 4A-C

claim: The density of OHCs in Fgfr1−/f;Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ was comparable to Fgfr1−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ and significantly decreased compared to control.
source: The density of OHCs in Fgfr1−/f;Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ was comparable to Fgfr1−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ (p > 0.94) and significantly (p < 0.001) decreased compared to control (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4F

claim: The density of OHCs of Fgfr2−/f::Fgf20Cre/+ embryos was comparable to control.
